settings.file_association_steps:
macOS has no "Default apps" pane — file associations live in Finder:

1. In Finder, locate any .apk or .ipa file
2. Right-click it and choose "Get Info"
3. Under "Open with", pick AppInfoTool
4. Click "Change All…" to apply it to every file of that type

signature.tool_hint: apksigner (Android SDK Build Tools) must be installed or configured to verify signatures. This does not mean the signature is invalid.
signature.subject: Certificate DN
signature.failed_code_modified_hint: codesign reports a code-hash mismatch (not a resource-seal mismatch). The usual cause is that this bundle was decrypted or repackaged: once the binary is decrypted or patched, the original signature cannot validate, while the app may still run. To double-check independently, unzip the IPA and run `codesign --verify --strict` on the same .app.
signature.failed_generic_hint: Signature verification did not pass. Read the raw output below: 'a sealed resource is missing or invalid' usually means files were added or removed; 'code or signature have been modified' means the binary was modified.
signature.failed_decrypted_hint: The main executable is decrypted (cryptid=0), which is the signature of a dumped build: once the code section is decrypted, the bytes the original signature covered have changed, so it can never validate. The app may still run, but 'the signature is valid' no longer holds.
signature.local_cert_sha256: Signing certificate SHA-256 (read locally from the v2/v3 block): {value}
signature.local_cert_hint: This is a structural fact, not a verdict: it proves which certificate is in the signing block, not that the signature is valid. Compare it with the fingerprint published by the developer.

install.subtitle: Install to connected Android devices over adb
install.drop_hint: Drop an APK / XAPK here, or click to choose
install.no_devices_hint: Connect over USB and enable "USB debugging" on the phone. For wireless, use "Pair over Wi-Fi" first.
install.pair_hint: On the phone: Settings - Developer options - Wireless debugging - Pair device with pairing code. The port is the one shown on screen, not 5555.
install.pair_invalid_code: The pairing code cannot be empty
install.connect_hint: Use the IP address and port shown on the phone's "Wireless debugging" screen (e.g. 192.168.1.35:37123). That port is NOT the one from the pairing dialog - a pairing port cannot be used to connect.
install.app_info_failed: Could not read package info (installation is unaffected)
install.log_open_failed: Could not open the XAPK container
install.log_install_failed: adb install-multiple failed with exit code {code}
install.uninstall_first_desc: Needed when signatures conflict - a repacked APK always does
install.connect_error_no_route: Cannot reach that address. The port is probably wrong, or the phone and this computer are not on the same network. (If you typed only the IP, 5555 is used - Android 11+ picks a random port for wireless debugging, so copy the one shown on the phone.)
install.connect_error_refused: The phone refused the connection. The port is wrong - a pairing port cannot be used to connect.
install.connect_error_auth: The pairing is no longer valid. Pair the device again.
install.pair_done_no_connection_hint: Go back to the phone's "Wireless debugging" screen and copy the "IP address & port" shown there, then use Connect with it. The port in the pairing dialog is only for pairing.
install.connect_error_after_restart: The port is reachable from this computer, but adb still cannot connect (the adb background process was already restarted). This usually means the pairing is no longer valid - pair the device again, then connect.

security.title: Security Detection

finding_texts.ios_usage_description: Info.plist declares {key} (a usage description is provided). Its presence only means the app **claims** it will use this capability; it does not prove the data was actually accessed at runtime.
finding_texts.ios_nested_usage_description: Nested bundle {bundle} declares {key} (a usage description is provided). Its presence only means that bundle **claims** it will use this capability; it does not prove the data was actually accessed at runtime.
finding_texts.ios_usage_description_cross_check: Cross-check against the APIs actually used: see the corresponding API clue entries in this report.
finding_texts.ios_photo_picker: Found system photo picker clues (PHPickerViewController / PhotosUI): the path where the user picks photos **does not require** full photo library authorization; this is a different access method from using PhotoKit directly.
finding_texts.ios_photo_picker_confirm_input_path: Confirm the actual input path: whether the user picks photos one by one, or whether full library access also exists.
finding_texts.ios_rule_a: Found full photo library access (PhotoKit) clues, but **no** system photo picker (PHPickerViewController / PhotosUI), which is the more restrained path. Listed as a medium-risk candidate for manual review — requesting full library access is not necessarily unreasonable (gallery management apps genuinely need it), but it is worth confirming whether a lower-privilege alternative exists.
finding_texts.ios_rule_a_manual_review: Manual review: can the system photo picker replace full library access? This item is a candidate for review, not a malicious verdict.
finding_texts.ios_ocr_capability: Image text recognition capability found: the Vision framework text recognition API. This only reports a capability; it is not a malicious verdict.
finding_texts.ios_ocr_capability_confirm_input_and_sin: Confirm the source of the input (user-provided / photo library) and where the result goes.
finding_texts.ios_rule_c: Image input, text recognition and network capability clues all appear together: a suspected path for sensitive data leaving the device. This is a high-risk candidate; static analysis could not prove that recognition results actually reach a network request.
finding_texts.ios_rule_c_manual_review: Manual review; if necessary, capture and verify traffic in an isolated environment.
finding_texts.ios_rule_f: No network upload characteristics were found within the current analysis scope (no hits for NSURLSession, multipart or common networking library markers). This does not mean the app has no network behaviour; it only means this scan found none.
finding_texts.ios_rule_f_runtime_traffic: To confirm, combine this with runtime traffic observation (not provided in this version).
finding_texts.ios_url_schemes: Info.plist registers {count} custom URL scheme(s): {schemes}. These are entry points that **external callers can use to launch this app** — a factual description of the attack surface; registering a scheme does not mean the handling logic is flawed.
finding_texts.ios_scan_coverage: API usage clue scanning covered {scanned} of {total} executables, {bytes} bytes in total. Every executable was covered.
finding_texts.ios_scan_coverage_gap: API usage clue scanning covered {scanned} of {total} executables, {bytes} bytes in total. Executables not covered: {uncovered}.
finding_texts.ios_photo_library: Found full photo library access API clues (PhotoKit), and Info.plist provides an NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription.
finding_texts.ios_photo_library_no_usage: Found full photo library access API clues (PhotoKit), but no NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription in Info.plist: the usage description is missing, so the system will refuse access at runtime — and the source of the access is worth confirming manually.
finding_texts.ios_camera: Found camera API clues, and Info.plist provides a camera usage description.
finding_texts.ios_camera_no_usage: Found camera API clues, but no NSCameraUsageDescription in Info.plist.
finding_texts.ios_rule_b: Both an image input source and text recognition capability were found: input ({sources}) and recognition (Vision text recognition). This combination may correspond to a normal feature (document scanning, translation, business card reading).
finding_texts.ios_rule_e: A background execution declaration, sensitive data read capability and network upload capability all appear together: background modes ({modes}), sensitive reads ({sources}), network (NSURLSession / upload). This combination may correspond to a normal feature (background backup, message sync).
finding_texts.ios_rule_d: App Transport Security allows arbitrary cleartext traffic (NSAllowsArbitraryLoads=true).
finding_texts.ios_rule_d_escalated: App Transport Security allows arbitrary cleartext traffic (NSAllowsArbitraryLoads=true), and image / recognition / network clues are present at the same time: sensitive data may travel over an unencrypted channel.
finding_texts.ios_privacy_info: Found a privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy); its declarations are listed below. Note: this is **declarative material** and does not equal actual data access proven by the system.
finding_texts.ios_privacy_tracking: The privacy manifest declares that the app tracks the user (NSPrivacyTracking=true).
finding_texts.ios_url_schemes_manual_review: To assess the attack surface, manually check whether the scheme handling logic validates the caller and whether it concatenates parameters straight into paths or SQL.
finding_texts.ios_scan_coverage_manual_review: For a more complete conclusion, manually inspect the executables that were not covered.
finding_texts.ios_photo_library_review: Confirm the actual purpose of the photos and how the user authorises them in the recognition/upload pipeline.
finding_texts.ios_photo_library_no_usage_add_usage: Manually check the call sites and the build configuration; add a usage description as Apple requires, or remove the capability.
finding_texts.ios_camera_check_purpose: Judge whether this is reasonable in the light of the capture, recognition and upload behaviour.
finding_texts.ios_camera_no_usage_add_usage: Manually check the call sites; add a usage description as Apple requires.
finding_texts.ios_capability_no_usage: Found {api} clues, but Info.plist has no {key}: the system will refuse the request at runtime, and the App Store review will reject the build.
finding_texts.ios_capability_no_usage_limitation: The presence of an API symbol does not mean it is called at runtime; the symbol may also come from an unused framework reference.
finding_texts.ios_capability_no_usage_add_usage: Confirm the call sites and add the usage description as Apple requires, or remove the capability.
finding_texts.ios_usage_without_api: Info.plist declares {key}, but no matching API clue was found in the scanned executables ({scope}). The declaration may come from a template, or the feature may be implemented in a way that leaves no scannable symbol.
finding_texts.ios_usage_without_api_relationship: The declaration and the absence of a symbol are both facts; the conclusion "this permission is unused" is not established.
finding_texts.ios_usage_without_api_limitation: Out-of-process pickers (PHPickerViewController), SwiftUI wrappers (PhotosPicker) and dynamically loaded code do not necessarily leave a scannable symbol, so a missing clue does not prove the feature is absent.
finding_texts.ios_usage_without_api_review: Confirm whether this declaration is actually used. If it is not, remove it: over-declaring a permission is itself a privacy problem and it makes the App Store privacy label inaccurate.
finding_texts.ios_rule_b_confirm_pipeline: Confirm the recognition input source and how the user authorises it (whether it goes through the system photo picker).
finding_texts.ios_rule_e_manual_review: Manually review what is uploaded in the background and what triggers it; if necessary, observe network behaviour while the app is backgrounded in an isolated environment.
finding_texts.ios_rule_d_manual_review: Confirm whether cleartext requests exist, and turn the switch off if necessary.
finding_texts.ios_privacy_info_cross_check: Manually compare the declarations against the API clues and the privacy policy.
finding_texts.ios_privacy_tracking_confirm_att: Confirm that the tracking purpose and the ATT authorisation flow match expectations.
finding_texts.ios_url_schemes_limitation: The scheme handling code was not inspected (no disassembly); “the entry point exists” and “the entry point is safe” are two different things.
finding_texts.ios_scan_coverage_limitation: The scan only extracts printable ASCII strings: system framework symbols in the dyld shared cache, non-ASCII literals and encrypted/hardened sections are all missed.
finding_texts.ios_photo_library_limitation: The presence of an API symbol does not mean it is called at runtime; the symbol may also come from an unused framework reference.
finding_texts.ios_rule_a_relationship: “The picker path is missing” is a **static inference**: the picker may also be used through the SwiftUI `PhotosPicker` or loaded dynamically, and those do not necessarily leave a scannable symbol.
finding_texts.ios_rule_a_limitation: The presence of a symbol does not mean it is called at runtime, and the absence of a symbol does not mean the feature is missing (dynamic loading, reflection, SwiftUI wrappers).
finding_texts.ios_rule_b_relationship: Image input → text recognition: the two clues co-occur, but they are not proven to lie on the same call path.
finding_texts.ios_rule_b_limitation: No disassembly was performed, so it cannot be determined whether the recognition module actually handles user-selected images or batch-scanned media files.
finding_texts.ios_rule_c_relationship: Image input → text recognition → network send: there is evidence for each of the three stages, but the hop “the recognition result enters the request body” is not proven.
finding_texts.ios_rule_c_limitation: No disassembly and no traffic observation; a framework reference does not mean the code is called.
finding_texts.ios_rule_e_relationship: Background execution declaration → sensitive data read → network upload: there is evidence for each of the three stages, but **not a single hop is proven** — it is not shown that the sensitive read happens in the background, nor that what was read reaches the request body.
finding_texts.ios_rule_e_limitation: `UIBackgroundModes` is a **declaration** and does not equal actual background behaviour at runtime; no disassembly and no traffic observation.
finding_texts.ios_rule_d_limitation: Allowing cleartext in the configuration is not the same as actually using cleartext; the per-domain exception settings are not expanded.
finding_texts.ios_privacy_info_limitation: The privacy manifest does not record actual behaviour; runtime data access would require the system App Privacy Report (not provided in this version).
finding_texts.ios_rule_f_limitation: Only ASCII strings are scanned (main executable plus nested executables). Code in the shared dyld cache, code loaded at runtime, and non-ASCII literals are outside the coverage.
finding_texts.android_permission_uncategorized: Another {count} permission(s) are not in the risk catalogue. Recorded as fact only: {names}
finding_texts.android_permission_uncategorized_manual_: Not being catalogued does not mean there is no risk: to assess these permissions, check them against the Android permission documentation manually.
finding_texts.android_permission_sdk23_conditional: {name} is declared with <uses-permission-sdk-23>, so it is only granted on devices running API < 23; the device version cannot be determined statically from the package.
finding_texts.android_permission_sdk23_conditional_lim: targetSdk is not a substitute for the device API level: the two can differ.
finding_texts.android_permission_sdk23_conditional_ver: For a conclusion, verify on a device running the target system version.
finding_texts.android_rule_a: Broad storage / photo library access found: {names}, listed as a medium-risk candidate for manual review. This analysis found no obvious image-related feature clues in the package that would explain it (such as system photo picker calls or image list screens).
finding_texts.android_rule_a_limitation: “The business purpose is missing” is a static inference: the business code may live in unscanned native libraries, a hardened shell or a dynamically loaded module.
finding_texts.android_rule_a_manual_review: Manually check whether the app really needs whole-disk file access; if not, consider the system photo picker (Photo Picker) instead. This item is a candidate for review, not a malicious verdict.
finding_texts.android_rule_d_escalated: The app permits cleartext (non-TLS) traffic, and image / recognition / upload clues are present at the same time: sensitive data may travel over an unencrypted channel.
finding_texts.android_rule_d_limitation: Permitting cleartext in the configuration is not the same as actually using it; the specific requests would need packet capture to confirm. Certificate pinning and trust anchors in the same config are not evaluated.
finding_texts.android_rule_d_manual_review: Confirm whether cleartext requests actually exist; turn the switch off if it is not needed.
finding_texts.android_rule_e: Background task, sensitive data access and upload call clues all appear together and corroborate each other: further verification at runtime is needed. Finding only a background task or a network permission is not malicious evidence.
finding_texts.android_rule_e_relationship: Background entry point + sensitive data source + upload sink: the three kinds of evidence co-occur, but “whether the app actually processes and uploads media data in the background” is not proven.
finding_texts.android_rule_e_limitation: No dynamic analysis was run, so the actual triggering and execution of background tasks cannot be observed.
finding_texts.android_rule_e_manual_review: Run it in an isolated environment and confirm after observing the network behaviour.
finding_texts.android_rule_f: No upload-related code characteristics were found within the current analysis scope (no hits for multipart upload, file upload APIs or similar markers). This does not mean the app has no upload behaviour — it only means this static scan found none.
finding_texts.android_rule_g: A non-image sensitive data source and upload capability were both found: {sources} → upload. This is a suspected exfiltration path; static analysis could not prove that the data read here actually reaches an upload request.
finding_texts.android_rule_g_relationship: The source API and the upload API both appear in the package, but they are not proven to lie on the same call path — whether the data actually flows into the request is not established.
finding_texts.android_rule_g_limitation: Co-occurrence is not data flow: the source may be read for an unrelated feature (analytics, fraud detection), and the upload may carry something else entirely. No disassembly or taint analysis was performed.
finding_texts.android_rule_g_manual_review: Review manually: check whether this data is actually sent out, and whether the user was told about it. This is a candidate for review, not a malicious verdict.
finding_texts.android_debuggable: The application declares android:debuggable="true". Anyone with access to the device can debug the app, read its memory and replace its code. Release builds must not set this.
finding_texts.android_debuggable_limitation: This is a manifest attribute, reported as declared. Whether this build was actually shipped to users cannot be determined statically.
finding_texts.android_debuggable_remove: Remove android:debuggable from the release build (it is normally injected by debug tooling or build variants).
finding_texts.android_exported_component: {count} component(s) are exported without an android:permission guard: {names}. Other apps on the device can invoke them.
finding_texts.android_exported_component_limitation: Exported is reported only when it is explicitly declared; components without the attribute are not judged (the default depends on the intent filters and targetSdk). Some exported components are meant to be called by other apps.
finding_texts.android_exported_component_review: For each component: add android:permission, or set android:exported="false" if other apps do not need it.
finding_texts.android_allow_backup: The application declares android:allowBackup="true": adb backup can export its private data on devices that still honour it.
finding_texts.android_allow_backup_limitation: Only an explicit allowBackup="true" is reported. The platform default is also true, but treating an absent attribute as the app's choice would flag every package. Android 12+ restricts adb backup further.
finding_texts.android_allow_backup_review: If the app stores sensitive data, set android:allowBackup="false" or provide explicit backup rules.
finding_texts.android_special_access: The package declares or references special-access capabilities: {sources}. These are high-privilege facts the user should be told about; declaring them does not mean they are abused.
finding_texts.android_special_access_limitation: This is a declaration/reference fact, not a behaviour finding: accessibility services, device admin and notification listeners all have legitimate uses (automation, password managers, watch companions). No runtime behaviour was observed.
finding_texts.android_special_access_review: Check what the app does with this capability and whether the user is told about it. This is a fact to review, not a malicious verdict.
finding_texts.android_rule_f_limitation_no_dex: No DEX content was read this time, so the confidence of the “not found” conclusion is incomplete.
finding_texts.android_rule_f_limitation_scope: String scanning does not cover native libraries, resources or code inside a hardened shell.
finding_texts.android_rule_f_runtime_traffic: To rule out upload behaviour, combine this with dynamic traffic observation (not provided in this version).
finding_texts.ios_native_symbols: The executable imports {count} system capabilities with a specific meaning: {symbols}. This only proves the binary **has the ability** to use them; it does not prove they are called, nor does it say anything about the arguments used.
finding_texts.ios_native_symbols_relationship: The symbols come from `N_UNDF | N_EXT` (undefined external) entries in the Mach-O `LC_SYMTAB` — dyld resolves them from system libraries at load time. A function the binary defines itself under the same name is not counted.
finding_texts.ios_native_symbols_limitation: Import does not mean call: the native code was not disassembled, so it is unknown which code paths call these functions. Implementations that issue system calls directly via `syscall()` or call indirectly inside libc do not appear in the symbol table.
finding_texts.ios_native_symbols_manual_review: To confirm the actual behaviour, analyse dynamically in an isolated environment (`dtrace` / Frida and similar). Importing `system` / `dlopen` alone is not a risk verdict — crash reporting, hot-fix and plugin frameworks all use them.
finding_texts.android_native_symbols: The native libraries import {count} system capabilities with a specific meaning: {symbols}. This only proves these libraries **have the ability** to use them; it does not prove they are called, nor does it say anything about the arguments used.
finding_texts.android_native_symbols_relationship: The symbols come from **undefined** (imported) entries in the ELF `.dynsym` — the dynamic linker resolves them at load time. A function the library defines itself under the same name is not counted.
finding_texts.android_native_symbols_limitation: Import does not mean call: the native code was not disassembled, so it is unknown which code paths call these functions. Implementations that issue system calls directly via `syscall()` or call indirectly inside libc do not appear in the symbol table.
finding_texts.android_native_symbols_manual_review: To confirm the actual behaviour, analyse dynamically in an isolated environment (`strace` / Frida and similar). Importing `system` / `dlopen` alone is not a risk verdict — crash reporting, hot-fix and plugin frameworks all use them.
finding_texts.android_ocr_capability: Image text recognition capability found: {parts}. This only reports the capability itself; it is not a malicious verdict.
finding_texts.android_upload_api: Upload-related APIs or code found: {parts}. This only proves the upload capability exists; it does not prove sensitive data was uploaded.
finding_texts.android_network_endpoints: Extracted from static strings: {parts}. Static extraction does not mean these were actually visited at runtime — a domain in a string may be a configuration value, an SDK address or a fallback endpoint that is never contacted.
finding_texts.android_network_client: Network client related code found ({parts}). This only proves the network communication capability exists; it does not prove data was transferred, nor does it say where the data went.
finding_texts.android_rule_b: Both an image input source and text recognition capability were found: permission/code clues ({inputClues}) and recognition capability ({ocrClues}). This combination may correspond to a normal feature (document scanning, translation, business card reading).
finding_texts.android_rule_c: Image input, text recognition and upload call clues all appear together: a suspected path for sensitive data leaving the device. This is a high-risk **candidate**; static analysis could not prove that data actually flows into an upload request.
finding_texts.android_ocr_capability_check_pipeline: Confirm the input source of the recognition feature (user-provided / library scan) and where the result goes (processed locally / sent over the network).
finding_texts.android_upload_api_manual_review: Manually confirm what is uploaded, what triggers it and the destination.
finding_texts.android_network_endpoints_verify: For unfamiliar domains, verify further with certificate pinning and traffic observation; an unfamiliar domain, the use of a CDN or encryption is not malicious evidence by itself.
finding_texts.android_network_client_manual_review: To confirm actual outbound traffic, combine this with certificate pinning, packet capture or enterprise-side traffic auditing; using some networking library is not a risk verdict by itself.
finding_texts.android_rule_b_confirm_pipeline: Confirm the recognition input source and how the user authorises it (whether it goes through the system photo picker).
finding_texts.android_rule_c_manual_review: Review manually first; you can capture and verify the actual outbound content in an isolated environment (requires dynamic testing, not provided in this version).
finding_texts.android_ocr_capability_relationship_code: The “code reference” comes from method_ids: the bytecode references these methods, but that does not prove they are called at runtime (the instructions in code_item were not walked).
finding_texts.android_ocr_capability_relationship_stri: All hits appear only in strings; no method_ids entry references them.
finding_texts.android_upload_api_relationship_code_ref: The “code reference” comes from method_ids: the bytecode references these methods/types, but that does not prove they are called at runtime.
finding_texts.android_upload_api_relationship_strings_: All hits appear only in strings (for example multipart/form-data is a request-header value, so it can only ever appear as a literal).
finding_texts.android_network_client_relationship_code: The “code reference” comes from method_ids: it proves the bytecode references these methods/types, but not that they are called at runtime (the instructions in code_item were not walked). “String mention only” may be a configuration value, a commented-out literal or an SDK that is never used.
finding_texts.android_network_client_relationship_stri: All hits appear only in strings; no method_ids entry references them — the presence of these literals does not mean the implementation exists.
finding_texts.android_rule_b_relationship: Image input → text recognition: the two clues co-occur, but they are not proven to lie on the same call path.
finding_texts.android_rule_c_relationship_package: The call instructions for text recognition and upload are **not in the same method body** (the co-occurrence is at the whole-package level). Reading a photo → image text recognition → building an upload request: there is evidence for each of the three stages, but “the data flow along the same code path” is not proven — the unproven hop is the recognition result entering the upload request.
finding_texts.android_rule_c_relationship_method: The call instructions for text recognition and upload appear **in the same method body** ({caller}); but co-occurrence within one method is not data flow: whether the recognition result is fed into the upload request is not proven. Reading a photo → image text recognition → building an upload request: there is evidence for each of the three stages, but “the data flow along the same code path” is not proven.
finding_texts.android_ocr_capability_limitation: Both code references and string hits **are not the same as a call happening**: the code paths were not verified by disassembly.
finding_texts.android_screen_capture: Screen capture capability found ({parts}). MediaProjection captures the whole screen content, which may include verification codes, chat messages and other sensitive information. This reports the capability only; it is not a malicious verdict.
finding_texts.android_screen_capture_limitation: MediaProjection requires an explicit per-session user consent dialog, so the presence of the API does not mean the app records the screen; it may only be prepared for a screen-sharing feature.
finding_texts.android_screen_capture_review: Check what is captured and whether the user is told about it. Screen sharing / recording are legitimate features in many apps.
finding_texts.android_network_endpoints_limitation: The string table does not contain every constructed URL (concatenation, encrypted configuration), nor does it reflect actual connections.
finding_texts.android_network_client_limitation: HTTP implementations using reflection, dynamic loading or a hardened shell do not appear in method_ids, so “no code reference” does not mean “no network communication”.
finding_texts.android_rule_b_limitation: No disassembly was performed, so it cannot be determined whether the recognition module actually handles user-selected images or batch-scanned media files.
finding_texts.android_rule_c_limitation: The association comes from multiple markers co-occurring, not from call-graph analysis; reflection, dynamic loading and hardening may all make the real path different.
finding_texts.android_permission_expired_limitation: The version condition is judged against targetSdk={targetSdk}; if the actual device version differs, the device is authoritative.
finding_texts.android_permission_expired_keep_observin: This declaration does not grant actual access capability under the current target version; keep it under observation.
finding_texts.android_permission_inert_check_legacy: Confirm whether the app still relies on the legacy behaviour of this permission; on a high targetSdk it is usually superseded by scoped storage.
finding_texts.android_permission_rule_limitation: A permission declaration is only an intent; it does not prove the app actually accessed the corresponding data at runtime.
finding_texts.android_exported_component_many: {count} component(s) are exported without an android:permission guard, including {names} and {more} more. Other apps on the device can invoke them.
finding_texts.android_shared_user_id: The manifest declares android:sharedUserId="{id}": this app shares a UID (and therefore a sandbox) with any other app signed with the same key and declaring the same sharedUserId.
finding_texts.android_shared_user_id_limitation: Whether another app with the same sharedUserId is actually installed cannot be determined from this package; only the declaration is reported. sharedUserId is deprecated since Android 10.
finding_texts.android_shared_user_id_review: Remove android:sharedUserId unless the data sharing is genuinely required, and review every app that declares the same value.
finding_texts.android_exported_component_weak: {count} component(s) are exported without an effective android:permission guard: {names}. The permission they declare is defined by this app with protectionLevel normal or dangerous, so any app can request it. Other apps on the device can invoke them.
finding_texts.android_exported_component_weak_many: {count} component(s) are exported without an effective android:permission guard, including {names} and {more} more. The permission they declare is defined by this app with protectionLevel normal or dangerous, so any app can request it.
finding_texts.ios_get_task_allow: The provisioning profile grants get-task-allow: a debugger can attach to the process, read its memory and replace code. Release builds must not carry this.
finding_texts.ios_get_task_allow_limitation: This is the entitlement declared in the provisioning profile; whether the build was actually distributed to users cannot be determined statically. Development and enterprise profiles legitimately carry it.
finding_texts.ios_get_task_allow_review: Ship App Store / ad-hoc builds signed without get-task-allow, and treat any build that has it as a debug-capable artifact.
finding_texts.ios_push_sandbox: The provisioning profile declares aps-environment="development": push notifications are bound to the sandbox APNs environment, which indicates a development-signed build.
finding_texts.ios_push_sandbox_limitation: The APNs environment is a property of the signing profile, not of the app logic; a distribution build uses "production" instead.
finding_texts.ios_push_sandbox_review: Confirm this build is meant for testing; production releases should be signed with aps-environment="production".
finding_texts.android_v1_only_signing: The APK carries no v2 or later signature block: only the v1 (JAR) signature is present (META-INF holds a matching .SF and signature block). v1 protects the digest of each entry but not the archive structure, so entries can be added without breaking it.
finding_texts.android_v1_only_signing_limitation: This only reports which signature schemes are present in the archive structure; it does not verify any signature and does not imply the package was tampered with. A v1-only APK can be perfectly validly signed. Whether the signature is valid must come from apksigner.
finding_texts.android_v1_only_signing_review: Sign with v2 (and v3 where key rotation is needed) — any modern build tool does this by default. If the package is v1-only, check where it came from.
finding_texts.android_unsigned: The archive carries no signature material at all: there is no APK Signing Block, and META-INF holds no matching .SF plus signature block. A package in this state cannot be installed as-is; it is typically a build artifact or a package whose signature was stripped.
finding_texts.android_unsigned_limitation: This only reports the absence of signature material in the archive structure. It does not judge the package malicious, and it does not replace apksigner, which is the only authority on whether a signature is valid.
finding_texts.android_unsigned_review: Confirm where this file came from. If it is meant for distribution, sign it with v2/v3 before installing; if it was extracted from a signed package, the original signature was lost in the process.
finding_texts.android_webview_bridge: A JavaScript bridge is exposed to WebView content (addJavascriptInterface): scripts running in that WebView can call the injected object. CAPTCHA, analytics and social-sharing SDKs use this routinely, so its presence does not mean the app itself defined a bridge.
finding_texts.android_webview_bridge_limitation: This reports that the API is used, not that it is reachable from untrusted content: the URL loaded into the WebView and any navigation allow-list are not evaluated. Most hits in real apps come from third-party SDKs (CAPTCHA, analytics, social sharing) — check the call sites in the evidence before treating it as the app's own design.
finding_texts.android_webview_bridge_review: Remove the JavaScript bridge unless it is required; otherwise restrict navigation to an allow-list of trusted origins and never load http:// or deep-link parameters into that WebView.
finding_texts.android_permission_without_api: These permissions are declared but no matching API call was found in the scanned code: {names}. The declaration may be left over from older code, or the code may live somewhere this scan did not reach.
finding_texts.android_permission_without_api_limitatio: Only the code that was actually scanned counts: native libraries, dynamically loaded DEX and third-party SDKs with unknown class names are not covered. A missing marker is therefore not proof that the permission is unused.
finding_texts.android_permission_without_api_review: Check whether the permission is still needed; removing an unused dangerous permission reduces both the permission list and the review burden.
finding_texts.ios_rule_g: Sensitive data sources and network upload capability appear together: {sources} on one side, network requests (NSURLSession / upload) on the other. Both stages have evidence, but it is not shown that the data actually reaches the request.
finding_texts.ios_rule_g_common: Location access and network upload capability appear together: {sources} plus network requests (NSURLSession / upload). Both are extremely common in ordinary apps, so this is reported at low severity.
finding_texts.ios_rule_g_limitation: This is a co-occurrence observation, not a data flow: it is not shown that what was read is sent. The specific request body would need runtime inspection.
finding_texts.ios_rule_g_manual_review: Check whether the app really needs these sensitive reads, and whether the data they return is part of an upload payload.
finding_texts.android_native_exec_stack: {count} native libraries mark the stack as executable (PT_GNU_STACK with PF_X): {names}. Data on the stack can be executed as code.
finding_texts.android_native_exec_stack_many: {count} native libraries mark the stack as executable (PT_GNU_STACK with PF_X), including {names} and {more} more: data on the stack can be executed as code.
finding_texts.android_native_exec_stack_limitation: Only the native libraries that were actually read are judged; libraries skipped for budget are not covered. An executable stack does not by itself mean the library is malicious — it only removes the NX barrier.
finding_texts.android_native_exec_stack_review: Rebuild the library without -z execstack (the NDK default is a non-executable stack) and ask the vendor for a fixed build.
finding_texts.android_third_party_sdk: {count} third-party service SDK(s) were found in the code: {names}. These libraries send data to their own servers; the list itself is an inventory, not a risk verdict.
finding_texts.android_third_party_sdk_limitation: Only class-name prefixes are matched, and only for the service SDKs in this catalogue: basic libraries (HTTP client, JSON, UI, animation) are deliberately excluded because they appear in almost every app. The reference count is the number of class names with that prefix, not the number of calls. An obfuscated or repackaged SDK will not be recognised. Only the DEX files that were read are covered — see the coverage entry for how many.
finding_texts.android_third_party_sdk_review: Check each SDK against the app's privacy policy: what data does it collect, and where does it send it. Remove the ones the app does not actually need.
finding_texts.ios_permission_request: The binary actively requests {count} system permission(s): {apis}. The evidence is the selector table (__TEXT,__objc_methname): this is code that will ask the user, which is stronger than a usage description in Info.plist — that only says the app is allowed to ask.
finding_texts.ios_permission_request_review: Check when each request is triggered and whether the user is told why. A permission the app never uses should not be requested at all.
finding_texts.android_rule_c_relationship_chain: The call sites for text recognition and upload are in different method bodies connected by a call chain ({path}, {hops} hop(s)). Both stages have evidence and they lie on one call path, but "the value flows from one to the other" is still not proven: the arguments passed across the call are not tracked.
finding_texts.android_permission_not_grantable: {name} is a signature-level permission: a third-party app cannot be granted it, so this declaration has no runtime effect. Its presence usually means the code was copied from a system app or produced by an obfuscator.
finding_texts.android_permission_not_grantable_review: Treat it as a code-provenance signal rather than a capability: find out where the code came from.
finding_texts.ios_entitlement_capability: The provisioning profile grants the capability entitlement {name} ({capability}). Unlike keychain or app groups, this one is rare in ordinary apps and widens what the app can reach.
finding_texts.ios_entitlement_capability_review: Confirm the capability is required by a visible feature, and that the profile is the one you intended to ship.
finding_texts.ios_ats_exception: Info.plist declares ATS exceptions for {count} domain(s); {weakened} of them actually weaken transport security: {domains}. ATS exceptions are scoped to those hosts and are a common, legitimate practice — but a host that allows insecure HTTP is a real downgrade for that host only.
finding_texts.ios_ats_exception_review: Check that every exception is still needed, and prefer removing NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads in favour of a valid certificate for that host.
finding_texts.android_webview_bridge_unsafe: A JavaScript bridge (addJavascriptInterface) is combined with file:// cross-origin access: any page loaded into that WebView can read local files and call the injected object — the classic local-file exfiltration path.
finding_texts.android_webview_extra_universal_file_acc: file:// pages may access any origin
finding_texts.android_webview_extra_file_url_access: file:// pages may read other file:// content
finding_texts.android_provider_exposed: {count} ContentProvider(s) are exported without an effective permission guard: {names}. Other apps on the device can query, and possibly modify, the data behind these authorities.
finding_texts.android_provider_exposed_grant_uri: At least one of them sets grantUriPermissions, so it can hand out per-URI access even to apps without the declared permission.
finding_texts.android_provider_exposed_partial: Some providers guard only one direction (readPermission or writePermission), leaving the other open.
finding_texts.android_provider_exposed_weak: Some are guarded by a permission this app declares itself at normal/dangerous level, which any app can request.
finding_texts.android_provider_exposed_review: Guard the provider with a signature-level permission, or set android:exported="false" if no other app needs it. If URI grants are required, keep grantUriPermissions but make sure the URIs handed out are scoped.
finding_texts.android_provider_exposed_limitation: A provider with no permission is reachable by any app on the device, but whether it returns anything depends on the data it holds. Providers disabled by android:enabled=false are still listed here — check the evidence.
finding_texts.android_deeplink: {count} link scheme(s) can launch this app from outside: {schemes}, across {components} exported component(s). A scheme by itself is normal (login callbacks, share returns); the risk is in what the target component does with the incoming parameters.
finding_texts.android_deeplink_review: Check that each scheme handler validates its input (host, path, parameters) before acting on it, and that the target component is the one you intended to expose.
finding_texts.android_deeplink_limitation: Only the scheme is listed. Whether the target component validates the incoming host, path and parameters cannot be determined from the manifest — that would need the code.
finding_texts.android_cert_pinning: The app declares certificate pinning for {count} domain(s): {domains}. This is what the configuration declares — whether the pins match the served certificate, and whether an expiration date has already passed, cannot be determined statically.
finding_texts.android_cert_pinning_review: Keep the pin set current (rotate before the expiration date) and make sure at least one backup pin is present — a pin set with a single pin will brick networking when the certificate rotates.
finding_texts.android_rule_c_limitation_graph: The chain comes from the call graph (shortest path, {hops} hop(s)), which is method-level only: the arguments passed along the chain are not tracked, so "the value flows from one to the other" is still unproven.
finding_texts.android_rule_c_limitation_graph_truncate: The chain comes from the call graph (shortest path, {hops} hop(s)), but the graph was truncated at the edge cap — longer paths may exist that were not found. It is method-level only: the arguments passed along the chain are not tracked.
finding_texts.ios_reference_tables: Decoded {classes} class reference(s) and {selectors} selector reference(s) from __objc_classrefs / __objc_selrefs. These are pointers the code actually uses, not words that happen to appear in the binary.
finding_texts.ios_reference_tables_no_action: No action needed: this entry exists so that other findings can say "the code references this class" instead of "the string appears somewhere".
finding_texts.ios_reference_tables_limitation: Only the main slice of each executable is decoded. Pointers in ARM64E binaries (PAC-authenticated formats) are not resolved — a wrong decode would look plausible but be garbage, so it is reported as unsupported instead.
finding_texts.android_packer: This package carries the native libraries of a known hardening packer: {names}. Packed apps load the real DEX at runtime, so the DEX- and string-based findings in this report may be incomplete — "not found" here means "not visible in the file", not "does not exist".
finding_texts.android_packer_review: Treat DEX-based conclusions on this package as a lower bound. For a definitive answer the app has to be run and its loaded DEX dumped — outside what this tool does.
finding_texts.android_malware_indicators: Capabilities that malware commonly combines are present: {signals}{reflection}. Each one alone can be legitimate (hot-fix, plug-in hosts, app stores), so this is a triage lead, not a verdict.
finding_texts.android_malware_indicators_review: Treat this as a lead: check what the app loads at runtime, where it comes from, and whether a shell command is reachable from external input. Dynamic analysis (running it in an isolated emulator) is the way to settle it.
finding_texts.android_malware_indicators_limitation: Static evidence only: the code references these APIs, it does not follow that they run, or that what they load is malicious. Hot-fix frameworks, plug-in hosts and app stores use the same dynamic-loading APIs. The loaded code is not in the archive, so it cannot be inspected here.
finding_texts.crypto_theft_risk: This package combines the capabilities needed to steal on-chain assets (USDT and others): {signals}. {addresses}A legitimate wallet has the same capabilities, so this is a **triage lead, not a verdict**.
finding_texts.crypto_theft_risk_addresses: In addition, {count} on-chain address literal(s) are hard-coded in the code — a common trace of clipboard address-swapping theft.
finding_texts.crypto_theft_risk_review: Walk the wallet flow by hand: does the app ever replace an address in the clipboard, does it ask for the seed phrase outside its own wallet UI, and where do the address literals come from? Dynamic analysis on an isolated device settles it.
finding_texts.crypto_theft_risk_limitation: Static evidence only: these APIs and literals are in the archive, but that does not mean they run, or what they are used for. Legitimate wallets contain the same wallet SDKs, clipboard calls and address literals (merchant or contract addresses), so **presence is not theft**. Strings beyond the scan budget were not examined. Well-known contract addresses (USDT and other stablecoin contracts, DEX routers, burn addresses) are excluded from the hard-coded-address signal.
finding_texts.crypto_theft_risk_blind_spots: Note: this static scan did not see everything — some DEX or native libraries were only partially read, or a native library looks encrypted/packed. The conclusion may be conservative: **not finding it does not mean it is not there**.
finding_texts.ios_jailbreak_toolkit: This bundle ships known jailbreak / kernel-exploit components: {components}.{kernel} No App Store app bundles these — they exist to bypass code signing and the sandbox.
finding_texts.ios_jailbreak_kernel_suffix: Kernel exploits give the code read/write access to the kernel, i.e. full control of the device.
finding_texts.ios_jailbreak_toolkit_review: Decide whether this is a tool you intentionally analysed. If it is an app from an unknown source, a bundled kernel exploit means it can take full control of the device — do not install it on a personal device.
finding_texts.ios_jailbreak_toolkit_limitation: Detected by component name only (framework directory names and dylib paths). A privately rebuilt exploit with a different name, or one linked statically with no residual strings, is not visible here. Absence of this finding does not prove the app is clean.
finding_texts.ios_repackaged: This bundle was modified after it was built: {dylibs} sit(s) directly in the .app root, outside Frameworks/. Apps built normally keep their dylibs under Frameworks/; a library at the bundle root is the standard footprint of an injected tweak or a re-signed repack.
finding_texts.ios_repackaged_review: If you did not inject this library yourself, treat it as untrusted code running inside the app's sandbox: it can read everything the app can read (including credentials and clipboard contents) and talk to the network on its own. Cross-check with the signature verdict — a re-signed or decrypted bundle usually fails verification as well.
finding_texts.ios_repackaged_limitation: Only dylibs sitting directly at the .app root are counted. A repack that merely renames the bundle, or one that patches the main binary in place, leaves no extra file and is not visible here — for those, the signature verdict is the only signal. Nor can static analysis tell what the injected library does.
finding_texts.ios_upload_api: Upload-related code found: the multipart/form-data construction used to attach files or binary payloads. This only proves the upload capability exists; it does not prove sensitive data was uploaded.
finding_texts.ios_upload_api_confirm_sink: Confirm what is uploaded and what triggers it. A multipart body is also how crash reports, log bundles and avatar uploads are sent, so the capability alone is not a finding.
finding_texts.verify_suspected_hint: How to verify: static analysis stops here. To confirm on a real device, install it and watch `adb logcat` (or the system log in Xcode's Devices panel on iOS) while triggering the feature in question, and check whether the matching network request or file read actually happens. This finding says the capabilities coexist - not that they were used.

evidence_texts.android_rule_f_scope: Scope of this negative result: {dex} DEX file(s) and {callSites} call site(s) were scanned; no upload marker matched.

native_symbols.shell_popen: run a shell command and read its output
native_symbols.exec_image: replace the process image and execute a program
native_symbols.dlopen: load a dynamic library at runtime
native_symbols.dladdr: look up the source of a symbol at runtime
native_symbols.ptrace: trace a process — a common anti-debugging or injection technique

verdicts.max_sdk: The permission declares maxSdkVersion={max}, while the app targets targetSdk={targetSdk}, so the system no longer grants it (ineffective on Android {next}+).
verdicts.min_api: A permission aimed at API {minApi}+, while the app targets targetSdk={targetSdk}: the effective model may be the legacy one; judge it together with minSdk.
verdicts.max_api_effective_above: targetSdk={targetSdk} is higher than API {maxApi}, so the effective behaviour of this permission is largely reduced by scoped storage.

permission_rules.read_media_images_description: Read photos (the fine-grained media permission introduced in Android 13).
permission_rules.read_media_images_risk_note: A routine permission for image apps; on its own it is not a risk. But if the app has no visible image-related feature, it falls under "broad photo library access without a business purpose" (rule A).
permission_rules.read_media_video_description: Read videos (the fine-grained media permission introduced in Android 13).
permission_rules.read_media_video_risk_note: As above: a routine permission for video apps; judge whether the purpose is reasonable together with the app features.
permission_rules.read_media_audio_risk_note: A routine permission for audio apps; when combined with image / OCR clues, look at the input source.
permission_rules.read_media_visual_user_selected_descript: Photos/videos the user explicitly selected (the partial photo access mechanism introduced in Android 14).
permission_rules.read_media_visual_user_selected_risk_not: This is the mechanism where the **user grants access to part of the media**, which is a different thing from full library access: its presence means the app only touches the photos the user ticked, and its absence is what suggests full access may be requested. It must not be lumped together with READ_MEDIA_IMAGES.
permission_rules.read_external_storage_description: Read shared storage (the whole-disk file access model on Android 12 and earlier).
permission_rules.read_external_storage_risk_note: On apps with targetSdk ≤ 32 this is close to "whole-disk file access"; from targetSdk ≥ 33 it is largely superseded by scoped storage (a leftover declaration has little real effect). Real hardened samples declare it with maxSdkVersion=32, so the version condition must be taken into account.
permission_rules.write_external_storage_risk_note: Writing to shared storage has largely stopped working since targetSdk ≥ 29; on its own it is not judged a risk, and only serves as corroboration in a broad-access combination.
permission_rules.manage_external_storage_description: Manage external storage (whole-disk file access; a permission Google Play restricts strictly).
permission_rules.manage_external_storage_risk_note: Spec 3.1 lists it as a "high-attention permission": usually only file-manager apps need it. When present it is recorded as a medium-risk candidate for manual review, not a direct malicious verdict.
permission_rules.camera_risk_note: Spec 3.1: judge it together with capture, image recognition and upload behaviour. When it co-occurs with OCR clues it is handled by rules B/C; on its own it is not escalated.
permission_rules.internet_risk_note: Spec 3.1: a network permission is not malicious by itself.
permission_rules.access_network_state_risk_note: A routine permission; like the other network permissions below, it is recorded as fact only.
permission_rules.foreground_service_risk_note: On its own this is a routine capability; spec rule E only escalates when it co-occurs with sensitive data collection and upload.
permission_rules.foreground_service_data_sync_risk_note: As above; when it co-occurs with sync and upload, look at its stated purpose.
permission_rules.receive_boot_completed_risk_note: A background entry-point clue and one of rule E's inputs; on its own it is not judged a risk.
permission_rules.wake_lock_risk_note: A clue for continuous background execution; on its own it is not judged a risk.
permission_rules.request_ignore_battery_optimizations_ris: A clue for staying resident in the background; on its own it is not judged a risk.
permission_rules.schedule_exact_alarm_risk_note: A clue for scheduled tasks; on its own it is not judged a risk.
permission_rules.query_all_packages_description: Enumerate the list of installed apps.
permission_rules.query_all_packages_risk_note: The app list is one of the sensitive data sources listed in spec 3.4; most apps do not need it, so its presence prompts a manual check of the purpose.
permission_rules.read_phone_state_description: Read the phone state (including device identifiers).
permission_rules.read_phone_state_risk_note: A device-identifier data source; watch for it co-occurring with upload logic.
permission_rules.access_fine_location_risk_note: Location is sensitive data; judge it together with the app features and the upload behaviour.
permission_rules.read_contacts_risk_note: A sensitive information source listed in spec 3.4; watch for it co-occurring with upload logic.
permission_rules.read_clipboard_risk_note: The clipboard may contain sensitive text; spec 3.4 lists it as a source of interest.
permission_rules.system_alert_window_risk_note: An overlay can cover the screen and capture taps — the classic "invisible overlay" abuse. Judge it together with where the overlay is shown; a floating ball or a call UI is normal.
permission_rules.request_install_packages_description: Request installation of other app packages.
permission_rules.request_install_packages_risk_note: Lets the app hand an APK to the system installer. This is the usual step for droppers and "update without a store" flows; an app distributed through a store rarely needs it.
permission_rules.access_background_location_description: Access location while the app is in the background (Android 10+).
permission_rules.access_background_location_risk_note: Background location is a continuous tracking capability; on Android 11+ it is granted from a separate settings page. Judge it with whether a foreground use case justifies it.
permission_rules.record_audio_risk_note: A sensitive source: judge it together with where the recording goes (upload) and whether a visible recording feature exists. Recording + upload is covered by rule G.

limitation_notes.ios_url_schemes_unreadable: CFBundleURLTypes could not be read ({reason}): the registered URL schemes are not covered.
limitation_notes.ios_nested_plist_missing: The Info.plist of {count} nested bundle(s) could not be read, so their usage descriptions are not covered.
limitation_notes.ios_executable_over_budget: {path} is {bytes} bytes, over the {limit}-byte scan budget: only the first {limit} bytes were scanned, and the uncovered part may contain clues that were not found.
limitation_notes.ios_executable_none_readable: No Mach-O executable content could be read: API usage clues cannot be checked. The usage-description and privacy-manifest conclusions are unaffected, but this is not a complete analysis.
limitation_notes.ios_executable_unscanned: {count} executable(s) were not scanned ({names}): “no clues found” on these files means “not looked at”, not “none”.
limitation_notes.ios_macho_scan_summary: The Mach-O scan covered {bytes} bytes in total and only extracted printable ASCII strings: symbols in the dyld shared cache are outside the coverage, and non-ASCII literals are missed too.
limitation_notes.ios_privacy_info_unparsable: A privacy manifest exists but failed to parse: {reason}. The declarations cannot be cross-checked.
limitation_notes.ios_privacy_info_absent: No privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy) was found: this is not anomalous by itself (only some apps provide one), but it means the declared data collection types cannot be cross-checked.
limitation_notes.ios_offline_static_analysis: This is an offline static analysis: the app was not installed, not run, and no network traffic was observed. No runtime evidence exists, so this report must not be read as confirming behaviour.
limitation_notes.ios_scan_truncated: Some scan ranges were truncated because of the budget, so the conclusions are not complete.
limitation_notes.ios_native_symbols_unreadable: The `LC_SYMTAB` of {count} Mach-O image(s) is out of bounds, so no symbols were read ({names}): “no imported symbols found” on these images means “not looked at”, not “none”.
limitation_notes.ios_native_symbols_stripped: Some Mach-O images have no `LC_SYMTAB` (the symbol table was stripped): their imported symbols cannot be checked. Binaries processed by the App Store are usually stripped.
limitation_notes.ios_native_symbols_semantics: The native symbols come from the Mach-O `LC_SYMTAB`: they show which system capabilities the binary imports, and do not show that those capabilities were called, let alone with what arguments. The native code was not disassembled.
limitation_notes.android_split_apk_base_only: This is a split package: the security audit only covers the base APK; the DEX and resources carried by the split APKs (language / density / ABI) were not analysed, so this result does not represent the whole installation set. Native libraries especially — the ABI split usually holds the copy that is actually loaded.
limitation_notes.android_manifest_unparsed: AndroidManifest.xml could not be parsed ({reason}): the permission and component audit cannot run, so this result only contains the readable part and is not a complete conclusion.
limitation_notes.android_dex_budget: DEX scan budget: {name} was only scanned for {scannedBytes} of {totalBytes} bytes ({percent}%). The remaining bytes were not searched, so clues inside them were not found. This is a deliberate upper limit, not a parse failure.
limitation_notes.android_dex_no_content: No classes.dex content was read: OCR, upload and network-domain code clues cannot be checked. The permission and configuration conclusions are unaffected, but this is not a complete analysis.
limitation_notes.android_dex_scan_summary: The DEX string scan only covered {dexCount} file(s), {bytes} bytes in total, and only extracted printable ASCII strings: non-ASCII literals, native libraries (lib/.so), resource files and code inside a hardened shell are all outside the coverage.
limitation_notes.android_dex_checksum_not_verified: {name} is over {limitMiB} MiB, so the checksum was not verified — do not read “no checksum anomaly reported” as “the checksum is correct”.
limitation_notes.android_dex_dynamic_loading: Runtime DEX loading clues (DexClassLoader) were found: code loaded at runtime is not inside the archive, so this analysis does not cover it.
limitation_notes.android_dex_structure_untrusted: {count} DEX file(s) have an untrustworthy structure ({names}): the string clues from these files are not a complete conclusion, and the uncovered bytes may contain clues that were not found.
limitation_notes.android_dex_method_not_traversable: {count} DEX file(s) have an untrustworthy structure, so no method reference analysis was done ({names}): “no code reference found” on these files means “not looked at”, not “none”.
limitation_notes.android_dex_method_budget: The method reference walk hit the budget limit; {names} were only partially analysed.
limitation_notes.android_dex_method_entries_unreadable: {count} method_ids entries could not be parsed during the method reference walk (index out of bounds or the string could not be read), so the references in those entries were not seen.
limitation_notes.android_dex_desynced_bodies: {count} method body(ies) were not instruction-aligned ({names}): the call sites in these method bodies are not trustworthy — the width table or the payload length may not match the actual shape of the file.
limitation_notes.android_dex_method_semantics: Method references come from method_ids (proving the code references these methods); call sites come from the invoke instructions in code_item (proving a call instruction exists). Neither proves it ran at runtime — no data flow analysis was done, so how arguments and return values are passed is unknown.
limitation_notes.android_dex_invoke_custom: There are {count} invoke-custom instruction(s): they reference call_site_ids rather than method_ids and were not parsed, so these calls are not within call-site coverage.
limitation_notes.android_container_anomaly: Container/parse anomalies may affect the completeness of the coverage: {anomaly}
limitation_notes.android_native_symbols_budget: Native library scan budget: {name} — this library was not analysed.
limitation_notes.android_native_symbols_not_traversable: {count} native library(ies) have an untrustworthy structure, so their symbol tables were not read ({names}): “no symbols found” on these libraries means “not looked at”, not “none”.
limitation_notes.android_native_symbols_skipped: {count} entries in the native symbol tables could not be read (name out of bounds or the entry crosses outside its section), so the symbols in those entries were not seen.
limitation_notes.android_native_symbols_not_scanned: {count} native library(ies) were not scanned at all (selection cap: 24 libraries / 96 MiB). The native-symbol conclusion does not cover them.
limitation_notes.android_native_symbols_truncated: Reading the symbol tables of some native libraries hit the budget limit, so only part of the entries were analysed.
limitation_notes.android_native_symbols_semantics: The native symbols come from the ELF .dynsym section: they show which system capabilities the library imports, and do not show that those capabilities were called, let alone with what arguments. The native code was not disassembled.
limitation_notes.android_native_symbols_unstripped: {count} native library(ies) have not stripped their symbol table ({names}): internal function names can be read. Release builds are usually stripped; this is a fact, not a risk verdict.
limitation_notes.android_offline_static_analysis: This is an offline static analysis: the app was not installed, not run, and no network traffic was observed. No runtime evidence exists, so this report must not be read as confirming behaviour.
limitation_notes.android_analysis_based_on_cooccurrence: The OCR / upload / background conclusions are based on string markers co-occurring; no disassembly or cross-method data flow recovery was done, and obfuscation or dynamic loading may change the conclusions.
limitation_notes.android_container_decoy_entries: {count} entries use a file entry as a directory prefix (e.g. {samples}). A normal archive never does this; it exists to break extractors that treat every path segment as a directory.
limitation_notes.android_manifest_attribute_start_nonstan: {count} elements declare a non-standard attributeStart (largest {largest} on <{element}>, the standard value is {standard}). A compliant reader skips the gap; one that assumes a fixed layout reads decoy bytes.
limitation_notes.android_manifest_attribute_size_nonstand: {count} elements declare a non-standard attributeSize (largest {largest}, the standard value is {standard}).
limitation_notes.android_manifest_namespace_chunk_nonstan: {count} namespace chunk(s) declare a non-standard size (largest {largest}, the standard size is {standard}).
limitation_notes.android_manifest_unknown_chunk: {count} chunk type(s) are outside the standard AXML element range: {chunks}.
limitation_notes.android_container_missing_primary_dex: The archive root has no classes.dex / classesN.dex. A normal build always has one; its absence usually means the main DEX was renamed, moved or encrypted.
limitation_notes.android_container_multiple_dex_files: {count} DEX entries: {names}. Multiple DEX files alone do not prove hardening — modern apps split because of the 64K method limit.
limitation_notes.android_container_dex_header_unreadable: {name} could not be read, so its DEX header was not checked.
limitation_notes.android_container_dex_header_not_standar: {name} does not start with the standard dex header (actual: {header}). Normal builds never produce this.
limitation_notes.android_container_unusual_native_library: {name} violates the lib*.so naming convention under lib/<abi>/.
limitation_notes.android_container_executable_in_assets: {name} is executable code inside assets/, which a normal build never ships.
limitation_notes.android_container_resource_table_missing: resources.arsc is missing while a DEX entry is at least 64 KiB. A normal build always has a resource table.
limitation_notes.android_container_resource_table_too_sma: resources.arsc is only {size} bytes, far below any plausible resource table.
limitation_notes.android_cleartext_policy_unknown: android:networkSecurityConfig could not be expanded (the resource, its file path, or the XML itself was unreadable), so the cleartext policy is not judged
limitation_notes.ios_entitlements_no_profile: No embedded.mobileprovision (App Store distribution keeps the entitlements inside the signature), so the entitlement list cannot be read statically
limitation_notes.ios_entitlements_empty: The provisioning profile was found but declares no entitlements
limitation_notes.android_native_hardening_not_provided: No native library content was provided, so the binary hardening attributes were not read
limitation_notes.android_native_hardening_some_without_re: {count} of {total} native library(ies) lack RELRO; this is not reported as a finding because it is a legitimate build choice (for example Flutter's libapp.so) and would otherwise flag every Flutter app
limitation_notes.android_container_dex_in_native_library: {name}: the content is DEX bytecode, not a shared library
limitation_notes.android_sdk_inventory_no_dex: No DEX content was provided, so the third-party SDK inventory was not built
limitation_notes.android_sdk_inventory_incomplete: {truncated} DEX file(s) were truncated and {failed} could not be read; SDKs that only appear in those regions are not listed
limitation_notes.ios_executables_truncated: {count} nested bundle(s) were not parsed at all (of {total} bundles that contain code), so their executables were neither scanned for API clues nor counted in the coverage figures above.
limitation_notes.android_signing_block_unreadable: The APK Signing Block could not be read ({reason}): the v2+ signature schemes are unknown, so "no signature block found" is not a conclusion this run can make. This is not a verdict that the signature is invalid.
limitation_notes.ios_permission_request_no_methname: No executable had a readable __objc_methname section, so active permission requests could not be determined. This is not a statement that the app requests no permissions.
limitation_notes.android_provider_exposed: A provider with no permission is reachable by any app on the device, but whether it returns anything depends on the data it holds. Providers disabled by android:enabled=false are still listed here — check the evidence.
limitation_notes.ios_reference_tables_unsupported: Class / selector reference tables could not be decoded ({reason}), so "the code references this class" cannot be distinguished from "the string appears somewhere".

notes.ios_macho_call_sites: Attributed {attributed} of {total} selector / class references to functions ({functions} functions in the binary). "Referenced" still does not mean "called": ADRP+ADD only loads the address, and what it is passed to is not visible statically. Note that `__objc_classrefs` mainly covers the app's **own** classes; system framework classes (`AVCaptureDevice`, `CNContactStore`) are usually reached through a direct `objc_msgSend` or `NSClassFromString`, so they are outside this dimension.
notes.ios_macho_call_sites_unavailable: No selector reference could be attributed to a function (no ADRP+ADD/LDR pair targeted __objc_selrefs, or no LC_FUNCTION_STARTS). Clues are reported as "referenced", not "called".

diff.title: Version comparison
diff.subtitle: Compare two analysed packages — field by field, and set by set.
diff.pick_hint: Only packages analysed on the Analysis page appear here.
diff.need_two: At least two analysed packages are needed.
diff.need_both: Pick a package for both sides to compare.
diff.platform_mismatch: Both sides must be the same platform — comparing Android with iOS only produces noise.
diff.unknown_field_hint: One side was not read, so these fields say nothing about what changed.
diff.unknown_set_hint: One side was not read, so the members of these collections cannot be compared.
diff.report_note: “Cannot compare” is not “no difference”: one side was not read, so those entries say nothing about what changed.
diff.report_scope_note: This report covers field-level and collection-level differences only. Security findings are not compared.
